title: QCI Connect: A Modular Full-Stack Quantum Computing Platform
authors: Eric Bertok, Hannes Busche, Florian Drinkler, David Emmanuel-Costa, Daniel Herr, Steffen Hien, Thomas Keitzl, Elisabeth Lobe, Alexandru Paler, Johannes Renkl, Martin Rymarz, Gary Schmiedinghoff, Peter K. Schuhmacher, Thomas Stehle, Benedikt Strobel, Hanna Tschakert, Adrian Vetter, Andre Waschk, Alexander Weinert, Lukas Windgätter
abstract: In a world of various competing quantum computing architectures, hardware-agnostic, full-stack platforms are necessary to bring the full power of quantum computing hardware to domain experts via the cloud. QCI Connect and its Software Development Kit provide a reference architecture for a full-stack platform with a modular design and open-source interface definitions, built to facilitate a community-driven application ecosystem. Here, we present its overall design and features, central interfaces, and lessons learned, both for users of the platform and as a reference guide for future developments.
summary: This paper introduces QCI Connect, a modular, full-stack quantum computing platform designed to overcome hardware fragmentation. It establishes a standardized architecture using an orchestrator and open interfaces to connect various QPUs and simulators. This allows domain experts to develop and run complex quantum applications regardless of the underlying physical quantum hardware.
main_problem: The fragmentation and lack of standardization across various competing quantum computing architectures and software stacks hinder the ability to bring the full power of quantum hardware to domain experts via the cloud.
main_result: QCI Connect provides a reference, modular, full-stack architecture that unifies disparate quantum hardware by separating concerns into distinct, standardized layers connected via open interfaces.
method: The platform employs a layered, service-oriented, and containerized architecture utilizing an orchestrator, message broker (Redis), and canonical representations like OpenQASM to manage job workflows across heterogeneous resources.
model_or_system: The system is QCI Connect, a full-stack platform designed to integrate various QPUs (e.g., trapped ions, neutral atoms) and HPC systems via standardized connectors and an orchestrator service.
key_observables: QPU status/occupation, job submission/result retrieval, and custom benchmark statistics like runtime and convergence metrics.
important_parameters: Job priority flags (low, medium, high); the canonical format subset of OpenQASM 3 used for internal communication.
main_assumptions: The design assumes that new components adhere to agreed system interfaces and task schemas for seamless integration; current hardware limitations restrict dynamic classical control within the canonical format.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the high-level architecture showing interaction between Physical, System, and Application Layers (Fig 1), component interconnections (Fig 2), job submission workflow via GUI/SDK (Figs 3-5), and the SDK's internal structure (Fig 6).
paper_structure: The paper details the necessity of a unified stack, presents the layered architecture (Physical $ightarrow$ System $ightarrow$ Application), describes core components like the orchestrator and message broker, specifies standards like OpenQASM, and outlines developer tools via the SDK/ALF.
why_interesting: It provides a high-level software framework that abstracts hardware differences, which is crucial for any theoretical work aiming to test algorithms on diverse physical platforms without rewriting the core logic.
analysis_basis: full PDF text, analyzed in chunks

figures.caption: Figure 1: High-level overview of QCI Connect. The software stack serves as a quantum computing gateway for users from academia and industry, within and out- side DLR. Major challenges lie in the simultaneous orchestration, scheduling, compilation, and data management for a wide array of simulators and hard- ware architectures with vendor-specific stacks. The four pink components in the top-right corner form QCI Connect SDK and are described in more detail in Section 6. The cross-layer concerns of error mitigation communicate between all layers. Benchmarking will be addressed in the future.

Figure 2: High-level architecture of QCI Connect, showing the containerised service stack hosted on a dedicated virtual machine inside the DLR network. User requests are routed through a reverse proxy to the frontend, orchestrator, and iden- tity broker. The orchestrator manages asynchronous task execution through a message broker and dedicated worker services for compilation, simulation, and QPU or HPC access, with persistent storage, centralised logging, and integra- tions with external identity, QPU, and HPC systems.
Figure 3: Screenshot of the overview of a quantum job prior to its submission via the GUI of the QCI Connect web interface.
Figure 4: Screenshot of the table of submitted quantum jobs in the QCI Connect web interface.
